lessons.changes: Shortened the poem to its core stanzas, changed 'perfume' to 'a rose'; questions rewritten with text evidence and a rhyme question; added a body-part-to-sense sort.

passage.title: My Senses Are Amazing
passage.text: My senses are amazing. They help me do so much. My eyes can see, my ears can hear, my skin and hands can touch. My tongue can taste the food I eat. My nose can smell a rose. My senses keep me safe from harm. My nose smells smoke, my skin feels heat, my ears hear fire alarms. Let's say all five together now: sight, hearing, taste, touch, and smell!

passage.title: The Sense of Sight
passage.text: Look before you leap! Your eyes help keep you safe. You look both ways before you cross the street. Your eyes are round like balls, so we call them eyeballs. Your eyelids close when you blink. Your eyelashes brush away dirt. Your eyebrows keep sweat out of your eyes. Look at a friend's eye. The black dot in the middle is the pupil. Light comes in through the pupil. The colored ring around it is the iris. In the dark, your pupils get bigger to let in more light. In the sun, they get smaller.

passage.title: The Sense of Hearing
passage.text: Your ears hear sounds all the time, even when you are asleep. Sound moves through the air in sound waves. You cannot see sound waves, but you can hear them. Sound waves can bounce off a big hill. Then you hear your voice again. That is called an echo! Inside your ear is your eardrum. When sound waves hit it, the eardrum shakes. Then your brain tells you what the sound is. Some sounds are loud, like a fire alarm. Some sounds are soft, like a whisper. If a sound is too loud, cover your ears to keep them safe.

passage.title: The Sense of Smell
passage.text: Take a deep breath. Air goes up your nose. The air has tiny bits in it, too small to see. These tiny bits make smells. When you sniff a flower, the tiny bits go up your nose. Your nose tells your brain, and your brain says, “That flower smells sweet!” Dogs can smell much better than people. When you have a cold, your nose is stuffed up, and it is hard to smell. Your sense of smell can keep you safe, too. If you smell smoke, there may be a fire. Tell a grown-up right away!

passage.title: The Sense of Taste
passage.text: Look at your tongue in a mirror. Do you see the tiny bumps? They have taste buds. Your taste buds tell your brain how food tastes. Cake tastes sweet. Pretzels taste salty. Lemons taste sour. When you taste something sour, you make a funny face! Some foods taste bitter, like coffee. Your nose helps you taste, too. When your nose is stuffed up, food does not taste as good. Try new foods! Your taste buds can learn to like new tastes.

passage.title: The Sense of Touch
passage.text: You can feel with your whole body! Your skin has nerves in it. Nerves are like tiny wires. They take messages to your brain. If you touch something hot, your nerves tell your brain, “Hot! Pull your hand away!” Your fingertips can feel very well. You can feel if things are soft or hard. A feather is soft. A rock is hard. Things can be smooth or bumpy, too. Your sense of touch helps keep you safe. Never touch a hot stove!

passage.title: Ray Charles
passage.text: Ray Charles was a famous piano player and singer. When Ray was a little boy, he got very sick. By the time he was seven, he was blind. He could not see at all. Ray went to a special school for children who were blind. He learned to read with his fingers. This kind of reading is called Braille. It has little raised dots. Ray loved music best of all. He used his ears and his hands to learn to play the piano. Ray said, “My ears are my opportunity.” People all over the world still love his songs.

passage.title: Helen Keller
passage.text: Helen Keller was a girl who lived long ago. When she was a baby, she got very sick. After that, she could not see or hear. Helen felt angry because she could not talk with people. Then a teacher named Anne Sullivan came to help. Anne spelled words into Helen's hand with her fingers. One day, Helen put her hand in cool water. Anne spelled w-a-t-e-r into her other hand. Helen understood! Everything has a name! Helen learned many words. She learned to read Braille and to talk. Helen grew up, went to college, and wrote books to help other people.
